title: John the Baptist, the Baptism, and the Genealogy of Jesus

verses.text: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene,
during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness.
He went into all the region around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins,
as it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: "A voice of one calling in the wilderness, 'Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.
Every valley shall be filled in, and every mountain and hill made low. The crooked ways shall be made straight, and the rough ways smooth.
And all humanity will see God's salvation.'"
Then John said to the crowds coming out to be baptized by him, "You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?
Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you that out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham.
The axe lies ready at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire."
The crowds asked him, "What then should we do?"
John replied, "Whoever has two tunics should share with him who has none, and whoever has food should do the same."
Even tax collectors came to be baptized. "Teacher," they asked, "what should we do?"
"Collect no more than you are authorized," he answered.
Then some soldiers asked him, "And what should we do?" "Do not take money by force or false accusation," he said. "Be content with your wages."
The people were waiting expectantly and were all wondering in their hearts if John could be the Christ.

John answered all of them: "I baptize you with water, but One more powerful than I will come, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.
His winnowing fork is in His hand to clear His threshing floor and to gather the wheat into His barn; but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire."
With these and many other exhortations, John proclaimed the good news to the people.
But when he rebuked Herod the tetrarch regarding his brother's wife Herodias and all the evils he had done,
Herod added this to them all: He locked John up in prison.
When all the people were being baptized, Jesus was baptized too. And as He was praying, heaven was opened,
and the Holy Spirit descended on Him in a bodily form like a dove. And a voice came from heaven: "You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased."
Jesus Himself was about thirty years old when He began His ministry. He was regarded as the son of Joseph, the son of Heli,
the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph,
the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai,
the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda,
the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri,
the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er,
the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi,
the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim,
the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David,
the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon,
the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah,
the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor,
the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah,
the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech,
the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalalel, the son of Cainan,
the son of Enosh, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.

context.author: Traditionally Luke, a Gentile physician and traveling companion of the apostle Paul, who also wrote the book of Acts
context.genre: Historical narrative — Luke dates John's ministry precisely, records his preaching, then moves through Jesus' baptism to a genealogy that runs backward to Adam
context.audience: Theophilus and a broad, largely Gentile Greek-speaking readership
context.setting: John preaches in the wilderness and "all the region around the Jordan," the rift valley that runs from the Sea of Galilee down to the Dead Sea. Luke opens by naming six rulers across Judea, Galilee, and the territories to the north and east, tying the scene to the wider political map of the Roman East.
context.custom: Ritual washing was familiar in Jewish life, but John's call was unusual: he asked people who already counted themselves God's people to be immersed as a sign of repentance, much as a convert might be. His farming picture was familiar to everyone listening: a winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind so the wheat fell to the floor and the light chaff blew away to be burned. Tax collectors collected for Rome and often took extra, and soldiers had a reputation for extortion, which is why John's answers to them are so specific.
context.timelineImmediate: Luke's opening verses place John's ministry in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, around AD 28 or 29. The chapter runs from John's preaching, through Herod locking him up, to Jesus' baptism and the start of His ministry at about thirty. Luke mentions John's imprisonment before the baptism, wrapping up John's story before turning fully to Jesus.
context.timelineBible: John is introduced with Isaiah 40:3-5, and Luke quotes the full passage, ending with "all humanity will see God's salvation," the line that shows the Gentile reach Luke keeps stressing. The voice at the baptism combines Psalm 2:7 ("You are My Son") with Isaiah 42:1 ("in whom I delight").
context.sparkNotes: Luke dates John's ministry by naming Roman and Jewish rulers, then shows John calling crowds to repent in practical ways: share your food and clothes, collect only what is due, take nothing by force. John tells the people someone greater is coming, who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, and is locked up by Herod for rebuking him. Jesus is baptized, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice from heaven calls Him the beloved Son. The chapter ends with a long genealogy that traces Jesus back through David and Abraham to Adam, "the son of God."

translation.meaning: Literally a change of mind, a turning around. John makes plain that it is meant to show up in how people live, which is why he immediately asks for "fruit" and then gives concrete examples to crowds, tax collectors, and soldiers.
An immersion or dipping. John's baptism is described as being for repentance and the forgiveness of sins, a public mark of turning back to God.
A wide fork or shovel used to toss threshed grain into the wind so the heavy kernels fall and the chaff blows away. John uses it as a picture of Jesus separating what lasts from what does not.

occurrences.note: Only here and in the parallel in Matthew 3:12.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's account of John's preaching in the wilderness.
Mark's shorter account of John's ministry.
Matthew's account of Jesus' baptism and the voice from heaven.
Matthew's genealogy, which starts with Abraham and runs forward, where Luke starts with Jesus and runs backward to Adam.

otBackground.note: The voice in the wilderness preparing the way of the Lord, quoted in full in verses 4-6.
"You are My Son" — the royal declaration echoed by the voice at the baptism.
The Servant in whom God delights — the second half of the heavenly voice.
The line from Adam through Seth to Noah, which Luke's genealogy traces in reverse.

mapCoords.placeName: Jordan Valley, near Bethany beyond the Jordan

commentary.note: Henry reads John's answers to each group as a pattern: those who profess repentance "must show it by reformation, according to their places and conditions." He notes soldiers in particular are "cautioned against the temptations of their employments." On the genealogy, he says Matthew shows Jesus as son of Abraham and heir to David's throne, while Luke shows Him as the Seed of the woman, tracing the line up to Adam and starting with Heli, whom Henry takes as the father of Mary.

Ryle stresses that John "exposes the uselessness of a repentance which is not accompanied by fruits in the life," and puts it plainly: "Doing is the very life of repentance." He also draws a sober lesson from the way Luke closes John's story with his imprisonment: the reward of God's servants is often not in this world.

JFB observes that the fruits John asks for are simply resistance to the sins that most tempt each group — tax collectors to extortion, soldiers to violence. On the genealogy, they lay out the long-running question: is this Joseph's line or Mary's? Some read "son of Heli" as son-in-law, making this Mary's line; others take it as Joseph's own, and JFB notes the difference of opinion has produced "much acute discussion."
